original_question: Do there exist achievable Cantorvals whose boundaries have positive Lebesgue measure?
target_in_paper: Problem 21 in Section 4 ("Cantovals, dual Cantorvals and their boundaries"): "Do there exist achievable Cantorvals with boundaries of positive Lebesgue measure?"
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's target very closely: it asks an existence question, restricts to achievable Cantorvals (not arbitrary Cantorvals), and asks for positive Lebesgue measure of the boundary. This is essentially the same problem as the paper's official formulation.
missing_details: The ambient space is the real line: the boundary is the topological boundary in ℝ, and the measure is one-dimensional Lebesgue measure on ℝ.
"Achievable" should be unpacked: an achievable Cantorval is a Cantorval that is an achievement set E(x) of an absolutely convergent real series, i.e. E(x) = {∑_{n=1}^∞ ε_n x_n : ε_n ∈ {0,1}}.
For a fully stand-alone formulation, the object C should be explicitly declared to be a Cantorval C ⊂ ℝ, rather than leaving the noun phrase implicit.

If maximum paper-faithfulness is desired, one may note the nearby contextual fact that the boundary of any Cantorval is itself a Cantor set; the question is about whether such a boundary can nevertheless have positive Lebesgue measure.
refined_question: Does there exist a Cantorval C ⊂ ℝ that is achievable—i.e. C = E(x) := {∑_{n=1}^∞ ε_n x_n : ε_n ∈ {0,1}} for some absolutely summable real sequence x = (x_n)—such that its topological boundary ∂C has positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure?
justification: The draft is aimed exactly at Problem 21, not at the neighboring Problems 19, 20, 22, or 23. In the surrounding discussion, the paper first recalls that the boundary of any Cantorval is a Cantor set, then says that although this removes topological ambiguity, one can still ask about the size of the boundary, and then states Problem 21 in precisely the form captured by your draft. The immediately following context records that all known examples of achievable Cantorvals have boundary measure zero and that all standard achievable Cantorvals have boundaries of Lebesgue measure zero, which confirms that the intended question is this narrow existence problem and not the broader adjacent question of whether every achievable Cantorval is standard. The only real omissions in your draft are the explicit meaning of "achievable" and the ambient interpretation of boundary and Lebesgue measure. The general notion of achievement set and the paper's working notion of Cantorval are introduced in Section 1.
